claims.text: Surface-energy gradients drive kinetic surface segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The volatility of Au and Cu contributes to their segregation and evaporation from AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Surface segregation overrides sluggish bulk diffusion in this quinary alloy.
Above a critical temperature, surface diffusion coefficients exceed bulk diffusion coefficients by orders of magnitude.
The PLD-grown, sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles initially have elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
Their initial FCC structure is metastable and governed by kinetic trapping rather than thermodynamic equilibrium.
The mechanism becomes dominant above approximately 800 K, with a predicted critical temperature near 850 K.
Au and Cu preferentially enrich at nanoparticle surfaces while other elements remain relatively concentrated in the core.
Au and Cu have sufficiently low surface or cohesive energies and sufficiently high vapor pressures to favor surface segregation followed by evaporation.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-5 nm particles amplifies surface-energy contributions neglected by bulk Gibbs-free-energy models.
Elevated temperature promotes structural disorder and atomic rearrangement in high-entropy-alloy systems.
Surface diffusion remains active even when bulk diffusion is sluggish.
Surface-driven mass transport reshapes initially non-spherical particles into spheres that minimize surface area.
Evaporation of surface-enriched Au and Cu causes particle loss and widening of the particle-size distribution.
Above the critical temperature, the remaining size distribution shifts toward larger particles because refractory cores coalesce.
Surface-energy gradients alone can reproduce phase separation and evaporation without bulk atomic mobility.
The proposed mechanism applies only below approximately 10 nm and fails for particles larger than approximately 50 nm or for bulk material.
Icosahedral particles transform at lower temperatures than truncated-octahedral particles because their surface energy is higher.
Surface-diffusion activation energies are generally lower than bulk-diffusion activation energies.
High entropy and sluggish diffusion would stabilize FCC structure and predict minimal structural change or nonselective coarsening.
